title: From scalar division to AX−XB=C
subtitle: G2 lecture 062000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded, source-grounded mathematical companion: independent derivations, worked examples, vector MathTex, reusable diagrams. Spoken source unchanged.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Suppose we know a number c and want to recover an unknown number x from the equation a times x minus x times b equals c.
body: Because numbers commute, the left side is a minus b, multiplied by x. If a and b are different, we divide by their difference and obtain one solution. If a and b agree, either there is no solution or there are infinitely many, depending on whether c is zero.
This elementary observation is the seed of the Sylvester equation, a central tool in matrix perturbation theory and, eventually, the Davis–Kahan estimates.
slides.takeaway: Cross-spectral differences play the role of scalar denominators.

slides.title: Keep the domains and codomains straight
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · Keep the domains and codomains straight
slides.lead: Let E and F be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
body: Let B act from E to E, and let A act from F to F. The unknown X maps E into F, and the known right-hand side C also maps E into F. Then A followed by X is a map from E to F.
So is X followed by B. Their difference is well-defined, even when E and F have different dimensions. The Sylvester equation says that A X minus X B equals C. This form of the equation is important.
slides.takeaway: The Sylvester unknown and residual are both maps from E into F.
slides.mathtex: X:E\to F,\quad A:F\to F,\quad B:E\to E,\quad C:E\to F

slides.title: Return to the scalar case
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · Return to the scalar case
slides.lead: Let a equal five and b equal two.
body: If c equals twelve, the equation becomes five x minus two x equals twelve. The difference is three, so x equals four. If c changes to negative six, x becomes negative two. The solution scales linearly with c because the equation itself is linear.

Now let a approach b. If their difference is one tenth and c is one, the solution has magnitude ten. If the difference is one hundredth, the solution has magnitude one hundred. We already see the stability issue.
slides.takeaway: Small scalar denominators create large solutions even without singularity.

slides.title: Eigenvectors reveal the same denominators
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · Eigenvectors reveal the same denominators
slides.lead: Self-adjoint eigenvectors transform the operator equation into scalar equations.
body: Take eigenvectors Auᵢ=aᵢuᵢ and Bvⱼ=bⱼvⱼ. Evaluate AX−XB=C on vⱼ and pair with uᵢ. Moving A across the inner product shows that the output coefficient is multiplied by aᵢ−bⱼ.
Every pair (i,j) supplies one independent equation. The difference can be negative; only its nonvanishing is needed to solve that coefficient.
slides.takeaway: Every eigenvalue pair creates one independently solvable scalar coefficient.

slides.title: What spectral separation means
slides.lead: The spectrum of a finite self-adjoint matrix is the finite set of its real eigenvalues.
body: If A and B have no common eigenvalue, every spectral difference a minus b is nonzero. Since there are only finitely many pairs, the smallest absolute difference is a positive number. Call it delta. In this setting, the Sylvester equation has one solution for every right-hand side C.

If the spectra overlap, at least one denominator vanishes. On the corresponding pair of eigenspaces, the Sylvester operator cannot recover an arbitrary component of C. A nonzero right-hand-side component there makes the equation inconsistent. A zero component leaves the corresponding part of X undetermined.
slides.takeaway: Disjoint finite spectra guarantee that all coefficient denominators survive.

slides.title: Ordered gaps and mere distance gaps
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · Ordered gaps and mere distance gaps
slides.lead: There are two different kinds of spectral separation.
body: One hypothesis says every eigenvalue of A lies at least delta above every eigenvalue of B. That is an ordered gap. A weaker hypothesis says every eigenvalue of A is at least delta away from every eigenvalue of B, without requiring A to lie entirely above or below B.
That is a distance gap, also called pairwise spectral separation. Either condition makes every scalar denominator nonzero. But the ordered condition also gives those denominators a common sign.
slides.takeaway: Ordered and pairwise gaps are different hypotheses; do not interchange them.

slides.title: The new operator on matrices
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · The new operator on matrices
slides.lead: The unknown matrix is a vector in a larger linear space.
body: The m-by-n matrices form a vector space of dimension mn. The Sylvester map X ↦ AX−XB acts linearly on that space. In orthonormal eigenbases, its eigenvectors are the rank-one maps uᵢvⱼ*.
This reformulation explains why an equation with unknown matrix X can be inverted by ordinary linear-algebra methods, even though neither A nor B is itself invertible.
slides.takeaway: The Sylvester map is an operator on the entire space of rectangular maps.

slides.title: Why we will need this in perturbation theory
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 062000 · Why we will need this in perturbation theory
slides.lead: Suppose we have two spectral subspaces and want to quantify the extent to which a perturbation couples them.
body: A residual block may measure the failure of an approximate eigenspace to be invariant. The desired correction block often obeys a Sylvester equation. The operators A and B represent restrictions to two spectral regions, and C represents the known residual.

If those spectral regions are separated, we can hope to solve for X and bound it in terms of C and the gap. This explains, at a structural level, why spectral separation appears in subspace perturbation estimates. The eigenvalue differences are not decorative assumptions. They are the denominators of the inverse problem.
slides.takeaway: Angle and residual bounds later invert this same cross-block operator.

slides.title: What to reconstruct
slides.lead: Begin with the scalar equation and classify the cases a different from b and a equal to b.
body: Verify the domain and codomain of every composition in A X minus X B. Then use orthonormal eigenvectors u and v to derive the scalar coefficient equation. Explain how the spectral difference becomes an eigenvalue of the Sylvester operator acting on rank-one matrix units.

Finally, distinguish three claims: the spectra do not intersect, their pairwise distance has a positive lower bound, and they are ordered on opposite sides of a gap. Identify which claim is strongest and why the distinction affects operator-norm estimates.
slides.takeaway: Rank-one matrix units expose the complete finite Sylvester spectrum.

slides.title: One operator, many scalar denominators
slides.lead: All finite-dimensional Sylvester facts can be reconstructed from the rank-one spectral blocks.
body: Start with AX−XB=C, choose orthonormal eigenbases, and compute (aᵢ−bⱼ)Xᵢⱼ=Cᵢⱼ. Nonzero differences give one solution; a vanishing difference creates a compatibility condition. The smallest nonzero difference determines conditioning in Hilbert–Schmidt norm.
For operator-norm estimates one needs more than entrywise inequalities. Track whether the gap is merely pairwise or has a common spectral order.
slides.takeaway: Invertibility follows from nonzero differences, while constants require norms.
